title: Chapter 75 — The Right Whale’s Head—Contrasted View
paragraphs: Crossing the deck, let us now have a good long look at the Right Whale's head.

As in general shape the noble Sperm Whale's head may be compared to a Roman war-chariot — especially in front, where it is so broadly rounded — so at a broad view, the Right Whale's head bears a rather inelegant resemblance to a gigantic flat-toed shoe. Two hundred years ago, an old Dutch voyager compared the Right Whale's head to a shoemaker's last.

But as you come nearer to this great head it begins to take on different appearances, depending on your point of view. If you stand on its summit and look at those two F-shaped blowholes, you would take the whole head for an enormous bass fiddle, and these spiracles for the openings in its sounding-board. Then again, if you fix your eye upon this strange, crested, comb-like growth on the top of his head, and look at this from the front, the whale takes on the aspect of some great, stubborn buffalo.

A great pity, now, that this unfortunate whale should be hare-lipped. The fissure is about a foot across. Sliding over this lip, as over a slippery threshold, we now enter the mouth. If we had not known it already, we would be informed by the vast rows of bristly bone plates hanging from the roof that this is the mouth of a Right Whale. A great number of these bones form what is called the baleen — through which the whale strains the water, trapping the brit and small creatures on which he feeds.

In old times, there seem to have prevailed the most curious fancies concerning these baleen plates. One voyager in Purchas calls them the wondrous "whiskers" inside the whale's mouth. Another, "hog's bristles." A third old gentleman uses the elegant language: "There are about two hundred and fifty fins growing on each side of his upper jaw, which arch over his tongue on each side of his mouth."

This reminds us that the Right Whale really does have a sort of whisker, or rather a mustache, consisting of a few scattered white hairs on the upper part of the outer end of the lower jaw. Sometimes these tufts give a rather piratical expression to his otherwise solemn face.

As everyone knows, these same "hog's bristles," "fins," "whiskers," "blinds," or whatever you please, furnish to the ladies their corset-stays and other stiffening devices. But the demand for them has long been in decline. It was in Queen Anne's time that whalebone was in its glory — the farthingale being then in fashion.

But now forget all about baleen and whiskers for a moment and, standing in the Right Whale's mouth, look around you afresh. Seeing all these columns of bone so methodically arranged, would you not think you were inside the great Haarlem organ, gazing upon its thousand pipes?

By this time you must have plainly seen the truth of what I started with — that the Sperm Whale and the Right Whale have almost entirely different heads. To sum up: in the Right Whale's there is no great reservoir of sperm, no ivory teeth at all, no long slender lower jaw like the Sperm Whale's. Nor in the Sperm Whale are there any of the blinds of bone, no huge lower lip, and scarcely anything of a tongue.
Look your last, now, on these venerable hooded heads, while they yet lie together. For one will soon sink, unrecorded, in the sea. The other will not be very long in following.

Can you catch the expression of the Sperm Whale's head there? It is the same he died with, only some of the longer wrinkles in the forehead seem now faded away. I think his broad brow to be full of a prairie-like serenity, born of a calm indifference to death. But mark the other head's expression. You see it has a look of hopeless, resigned defiance.
